content: Rheumatic fever is a systemic immune-mediated disease that can develop following an infection with Streptococcus bacteria, such as strep throat or scarlet fever. It primarily affects the heart, joints, blood vessels, and brain. The disease can be classified as either acute or chronic, depending on the duration of symptoms. The most common cause of rheumatic fever is an infection with Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. If untreated, rheumatic fever can lead to valvular heart diseases, including mitral or aortic valve stenosis, regurgitation, and myocarditis. These complications may result in reduced cardiac output, pulmonary edema, and ultimately heart failure. However, in cases without carditis, the prognosis is excellent, with no residual heart disease. Conversely, patients with preexisting heart disease have a poor prognosis, often leading to mortality. Common complications include arrhythmias, systemic emboli, and stroke. Physical examination findings often include fever, cardiac murmurs, and erythema marginatum. Diagnostic tools such as echocardiography and radiography are useful, and the Jones criteria are employed to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment typically involves antibiotics to eradicate the Streptococcus infection and anti-inflammatory medications, such as aspirin and corticosteroids, to reduce inflammation. Long-term penicillin therapy is crucial to prevent recurrence and further complications. The term rheumatic fever was first introduced by the French physician Guillaume de Baillou in the early 1600s. In 1944, Dr. T. Duckett Jones published the first set of diagnostic criteria for the disease. Rheumatic fever results from an autoimmune response triggered by a virulent Streptococcus pyogenes infection in individuals previously sensitized by prior infections. During the infection, antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages, present bacterial antigens to helper T cells, which then activate B cells to produce antibodies against the Streptococcus cell wall. Unfortunately, these antibodies also cross-react with myocardial and joint tissues, leading to the clinical manifestations of rheumatic fever. The primary cause of rheumatic fever is an infection with Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes. It is essential to differentiate rheumatic fever from other diseases that present with fever, skin rash, nausea, and fatigue, such as typhoid fever, malaria, Lassa fever, Ebola, and scarlet fever. The incidence of rheumatic fever in developed countries, such as the USA and Canada, was approximately 20–40 cases per 100,000 individuals between 1970 and 1990, with sporadic cases of rheumatic heart disease. Over the past two decades, the prevalence has decreased to 5–20 cases per 100,000 in Canada and fewer than 5 cases per 100,000 in the USA, with no new cases of rheumatic heart disease reported. However, rheumatic fever remains endemic in many developing countries and is most commonly observed in children aged 5–15 years. Risk factors for developing rheumatic fever include low socioeconomic status, inadequate healthcare access, and poor sanitation. Screening for rheumatic fever is critical, as many cases of rheumatic heart disease are subclinical. Echocardiography is recommended in high-risk populations, and any abnormalities detected should prompt further cardiac evaluation and antimicrobial therapy. If left untreated, rheumatic fever can progress to complications such as arrhythmias, systemic emboli, and endocarditis, which may lead to heart failure. Common complications include valvular stenosis, carditis, and stroke. The prognosis is generally poor if the disease is not treated. The Jones criteria are used to diagnose rheumatic fever. A definitive diagnosis requires evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection, such as elevated or rising antistreptolysin O titers or DNAase, along with either two major criteria or one major and two minor criteria. A thorough patient history is essential, focusing on prior rheumatic fever infections, family history of rheumatic fever, and recent streptococcal infections. Common symptoms include fever, nosebleeds, and skin rash. Physical examination findings often include fever, Sydenham's chorea, cardiac murmurs, and erythema marginatum. Laboratory findings consistent with rheumatic fever include elevated inflammatory markers, evidence of streptococcal infection, and elevated or rising antistreptolysin O antibody titers. On electrocardiogram, rheumatic fever may present with PR interval prolongation, conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, or P mitrale, depending on the structures involved and the extent of cardiac damage. Chest X-rays may reveal cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema secondary to heart failure. Echocardiography is helpful in diagnosing carditis and monitoring the progression of valvular defects associated with rheumatic fever. The cornerstone of treatment for rheumatic fever is antimicrobial therapy combined with anti-inflammatory medications. Penicillin is the drug of choice, but ampicillin and amoxicillin are equally effective. Supportive therapy includes the continuous use of low-dose antibiotics, such as penicillin, sulfadiazine, or erythromycin, to prevent recurrence. Primary prevention strategies include reducing exposure to Group A Streptococci and antibiotic prophylaxis for streptococcal pharyngitis. Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G and oral penicillin V are the recommended antibiotics for treating Group A streptococcal infections in the absence of penicillin allergy. Secondary prevention strategies involve antibiotic prophylaxis immediately following the treatment of rheumatic fever. The duration of prophylactic treatment depends on the degree of cardiac damage caused by rheumatic fever.
